main_article.title: Q&A: ‘Godzilla-level’ El Niño is causing extreme weather – our environment writers answer your questions – live
main_article.summary_html:
Guardian reporters Jonathan Watts and Gabrielle Canon are online answering your questions on climate and extreme weather from what to expect this winter in the UK to the increasing risk of natural disasters.

saltybacon asks: Doesn’t the hype, as in “Godzilla-level” just turn a lot of people off the whole issue? Why do the warnings always have to be so over top? And what will be said if very little actually happens away from the norm? Keeping in mind the norm has always been wildfires, floods and storms since time began.

Gabby says: I hear you - the names can be a little much. These colloquialisms aren’t coming from scientists who are still describing this El Niño as a “very strong” event. But I think what people who use these terms - whether they are journalists or emergency managers or others in communication roles - are trying to convey is the startling leap we are seeing in the numbers this year. It’s a challenge to balance putting that into perspective, without causing either undue alarm or contributing to messaging fatigue. But here’s what we know: this El Niño is well on its way to being off the charts and it’s expected to strengthen over the next few months. An El Niño is classified by how many degrees Celsius monthly sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific warm.

El Niño is declared after that region rises 0.5C above normal. As of 21 September, the daily anomaly in that region reached over 3C - setting a new record. This is alarming because temperatures are exceptionally high - and still climbing. There is of course some nuance needed here. Scientists have had to create a new system to measure these temperatures in recent years because overall the oceans are warmer.

Jon says: The UK Met Office has warned this El Niño will be the largest in memory and probably the biggest since the 19th century. The impacts will be strongest around its peak, which is expected in November or December. “We expect the influence of El Niño to start to increase the chances of wetter, stormier conditions for northwest Europe, including the UK, in the coming autumn and early winter. But the Met Office has distanced itself from some of the wilder headlines, such as “El Niño to smash Brits with polar vortex of snow and storms in dire warning.”

Rather more cautiously, its meteorologists observe: “El Niño can increase the likelihood of wetter, stormier and generally milder conditions in the UK during late autumn and early winter. Later in winter, following the peak of El Niño, the stratospheric polar vortex can become weaker. This may raise the chance of Sudden Stratospheric Warming events, which can increase the potential for cold weather. These are shifts in probability rather than guarantees. El Niño does not determine individual weather events, and the current forecast does not support the suggestion that the UK is about to be “smashed” by widespread snow associated with changes to the polar vortex.”
